Photo: Pinar Alver / Shutterstock.com Chinese lending: what it costs and who originates it Chinese credit to Africa has become substantially more expensive. In a piece for ODI Global’s This Week in Macroeconomics , I discuss how the average interest rate on Chinese loans to African countries rose from 2.5% in 2020 to 5.7% in 2024. Part of this was imported: because many Chinese loans are denominated in US dollars, US rate hikes passed straight through. The rest reflects choices made in Beijing: a shift from policy bank lending to commercial lending by banks such as ICBC and Bank of China; the repricing of risk after a wave of debt distress; more expensive rescue lending; and a move towards “small and beautiful” projects with shorter repayment periods and market-aligned rates. The analysis also highlights that borrowing in renminbi remains far less costly than in dollars, prompting several African countries to pilot local-currency arrangements.
On how these loans are priced and secured, David Landry and Keyi Tang challenge the idea that Chinese capital is “patient” . The mainstream view is that China tolerates high risk to maintain diplomatic ties, win contracts for its firms and secure strategic resources. Drawing on more than 2,000 Chinese loans committed between 2000 and 2021 and over 75 interviews across China, Africa and Latin America, they find a hard-nosed risk management instead. Chinese loans often combine two or more protective instruments – such as resource collateral, credit insurance and higher interest margines – which serve as complements rather than substitutes. This also helps explain the rising rates discussed above, confirming that Chinese lenders have long priced for risk.
What matters is not only how much loans cost, but also how they are originated. Keyi Tang and Hong Zhang describe a model of “delegated origination” . Chinese state-owned contractors pitch projects directly to host-country politicians, secure their backing and then lobby the policy banks for financing. Lending is frequently driven from the bottom up by contractors’ commercial interests rather than handed down through Beijing’s formal diplomatic channels. For borrowing governments, the practical lesson is to screen projects and procure competitively at home rather than rely on the lender to exercise due diligence.
With Western aid budgets shrinking and debt distress spreading, how does Beijing see its own role? Zhou Taidong and Yu Lu offer a view from Chinese policy scholars . They describe international development cooperation moving from contraction to reshaping: traditional aid is being cut and sovereign debt crises are mounting, while the Global South is gaining a stronger voice. China’s response, as they set it out, is to promote the Global Development Initiative (GDI), move towards market-oriented green and digital investment, and build South-South knowledge platforms.
Read alongside the lending pieces above, this shows how Beijing presents the shift to commercial, market-aligned finance: as a new model of cooperation. However, this shift risks having a negative impact on the poorest, most aid-dependent economies that international financial markets deem uncreditworthy.
By the standard measure – manufacturing value added as a share of GDP – China has deindustrialised: the share has fallen about seven percentage points from its mid-2000s peak. Richard Baldwin argues this is a “phantom deindustrialisation” . China makes more goods than ever. Fierce domestic competition and fast productivity growth have pushed prices down so quickly that manufacturing’s nominal share of GDP shrinks even as physical output grows. This distinction matters in the “China Shock 2.0” debate, because a falling share of nominal value added is not a falling share of world production.
Pharmaceuticals show that China is moving up the value chain as well as producing more. Panle Jia Barwick, Hongyuan Xia and Tianli Xia trace China’s shift from pharmaceutical “free rider” to global innovator .
In 2010, China accounted for less than 8% of global clinical trials. By 2020, it had overtaken the United States in the number of clinical trials registered each year. The main driver, they find, was a regulatory reform that expanded the market for innovative drugs. After the reform, drug trials rose by 86% and became noticeably more novel. The lesson for other countries is that a larger, guaranteed market can do as much for innovation as direct subsidies.
For developing countries, cheap Chinese goods lower costs for consumers and for firms that use them as inputs. They also make it harder to build domestic manufacturing. Adam Tooze questions how far that second point goes. He takes on the “China squeeze” argument of Shoumitro Chatterjee, Arvind Subramanian and Devesh Kapur, who say that China’s persistent surplus in low-skill exports is blocking industrialisation elsewhere, notably in India. Tooze argues that India’s manufacturing shortfall owes more to domestic political economy, including low female labour force participation and restrictive regulation. The practical lesson holds either way: waiting for China to cede export space is not a development strategy.
Most research on Global China focuses on loans, infrastructure and firms. A growing body of work asks who works in the factories and who loses land to them. Mingwei Huang and Robert Wyrod set out a feminist framework for Global China studies . They argue that the macro focus misses gendered labour, racial hierarchies, social reproduction and everyday “intimacies” across Africa and the wider Global South.
For governments courting Chinese manufacturing investment, the clear policy takeaway is to integrate gender-disaggregate impact assessments and community safeguards into zone planning from the outset.

The study assesses MA’s additionality and highlights its catalytic role in driving structural transformation.
